_meta.why_v2: v1 diagnosed insomnia, assigned a 1-10 sleep-health score, and invented precise physiology (melatonin suppression windows, caffeine half-life cutoffs, an 'evidence-based' circadian schedule) from a handful of checkboxes. v2 frames every recommendation as an experiment to try and observe; sleep_score is force-nulled server-side; melatonin/medication recommendations are banned outright.
_meta.why_v2_1: v2's first live output still fused separately-supplied facts into one claim ('racing thoughts' selected + '3 AM waking' reported -> 'the racing thoughts... make the 3 AM wakefulness the most useful thing to test') and used population claims ('roughly 20 minutes feels natural for most people'). Both banned. The protocol had also drifted into a 3-step checklist run at once instead of one experiment; replaced with ONE EXPERIMENT AT A TIME (one primary + up to two sequenced 'try next' full cards). protocol cap 4 -> 3, code-enforced.
_meta.why_v2_2: v2.1's live test (the tool's own shift-work example: rotating nights, partner up at 9 AM, near-total sleep loss on switch-back days) found the one-experiment rule wasn't actually being enforced structurally — it still produced 2 'most useful variables', 2 quick wins, and a primary experiment PLUS a switch-back intervention PLUS an environmental audit: 3 full protocol cards again, just relabeled. Worse, the switch-back 'experiment' had drifted into consequential sleep-restriction advice ('choose a single wake time you will hold both days even if sleep was short', 'do not compensate with a long nap') for someone reporting near-total sleep loss during a shift transition -- exactly the case where the tool should recognize it has exceeded ordinary sleep-hygiene experimentation. Fixes, both structural and content: (1) PRIMARY EXPERIMENT ENFORCEMENT replaces ONE EXPERIMENT AT A TIME -- protocol is now EXACTLY ONE entry (cap dropped 3 -> 1, code-enforced in validateResult), quick_wins must support that same experiment, and every other plausible variable goes into a new 'try_next' field: at most 2 SHORT NAMED possibilities with explicitly no instructions, rendered as chips, not cards -- 'a protocol card disguised as one experiment' is now impossible by construction, not just discouraged. (2) SHIFT WORK AND SEVERE SLEEP LOSS: an explicit banned-instruction list (hold a wake time despite little sleep, skip compensatory sleep/naps, stay awake to force adjustment, rapid re-timing, light/melatonin/medication circadian manipulation) plus a required 3-step alternative (identify the one low-risk testable variable / state plainly in diagnosis or key_issues that the transition itself deserves professional guidance / name what to bring to that conversation). (3) The DO NOT COMBINE rule was widened to explicitly cover the diagnosis field's OPENING sentence, not just later ones -- the original bug had a hedged 'may be' two sentences after an unhedged causal claim in sentence one; the visitor reads sentence one first. (4) Schedule can no longer render half-populated: a schedule needs BOTH a real bedtime and a real wake_time (a placeholder string like 'to be determined' is explicitly rejected by a regex, not just relies on the model not writing one) or the whole schedule collapses to null -- both backend (validateResult) and frontend (render guard) now require this. (5) UI: submit button 'Build My Sleep Protocol' -> 'Build my sleep experiment' (sa_build_btn + sa_building, all 13 languages).
_meta.how_to_regression_diff: Re-run (npm run check:golden sleep-architect) — TEST IN A NON-ENGLISH LANGUAGE. Diff for QUALITY not exact match: HTTP 200. GUARDS: (1) protocol[].phase MUST be an English token (immediate|week1|ongoing|environment). (2) protocol MUST be exactly 1 entry (code-enforced .slice(0,1) in validateResult — this is deliberate, never raise it back up without re-reading why_v2_2 above). (3) try_next capped at 2, each entry SHORT (a few words naming a variable, not a paragraph of steps) — if try_next entries start reading like protocol cards, that's the 'disguised second experiment' bug back. (4) quick_wins capped at 2 and must read as supporting protocol[0], never a second intervention. (5) key_issues/protocol.actions capped at 4. (6) no-inner-double-quote rule. (7) sleep_score MUST be null in every case. (8) schedule is null whenever bedtime or wake_time is missing OR is a placeholder string (case 2 has schedule: null; verify a case with 'to be determined' or similar in either field also comes back null, not half-populated). (9) eyeball wording for: the diagnosis's FIRST sentence must be as hedged as its later sentences — no unhedged causal claim followed by a correctly-hedged one; no 'most/many people' population claims or invented time thresholds; for a shift-work / severe-sleep-loss case (case 3), the primary experiment must never restrict, delay, discourage, or forbid sleep, and the diagnosis or key_issues must explicitly name the severe transition as worth a clinician's attention. No gate catches wording drift on any of this — this file is the only record of what 'good' looks like. DO NOT reverse: phase English pin; the protocol=1 cap; the try_next 'names only' design; the no-inner-quote rule; the sa_disclaimer i18n line; the null sleep_score; the conditional (not automatic) schedule; the shift-work banned-instruction list.

input.freeform: Ich liege oft stundenlang wach und grüble über die Arbeit. Trinke nachmittags Kaffee.

output.diagnosis: Du beschreibst, dass du oft stundenlang wach liegst und über die Arbeit grübelst – obwohl dein angestrebtes Schlaffenster von 23:30 bis 07:00 Uhr rund 7,5 Stunden umfasst, schläfst du nach eigenen Angaben tatsächlich etwa 5 Stunden. Ob das Grübeln das Einschlafen erschwert oder ob andere Faktoren dabei eine Rolle spielen, lässt sich aus diesen Angaben nicht feststellen. Zwei Variablen lohnen sich als erstes zu testen: das Gedankenkarussell vor dem Schlafen und die Bildschirmnutzung im Bett.
key_issues: Gemeldetes Muster: stundenlange Grübelei über die Arbeit beim Zubettgehen
Prüfenswert: ob Bildschirmnutzung kurz vor dem Schlafen das Einschlafen beeinflusst
Prüfenswert: ob nachmittäglicher Kaffeekonsum mit dem Schlaf zusammenhängt
Noch unbekannt: was das nächtliche Aufwachen auslöst
quick_wins: Lege heute Abend Handy und Bildschirme mindestens 30 Minuten vor 23:30 Uhr weg – nicht als Lösung, sondern um zu beobachten, ob das Einschlafen sich dadurch verändert.
Halte Stift und Zettel neben dem Bett bereit, um beim Zubettgehen offene Gedanken kurz aufzuschreiben – das ist Teil des Experiments, nicht eine Garantie.

protocol.title: Gedanken-Ablage vor dem Schlafen testen
protocol.description: Du berichtest, dass du grübelnd über die Arbeit liegst – es lohnt sich zu testen, ob ein kurzer schriftlicher Gedanken-Ablage-Moment vor dem Zubettgehen dazu beiträgt, dass du schneller zur Ruhe kommst. Das beantwortet die Frage: Verändert sich das Einschlafen, wenn Gedanken vor dem Schlafengehen auf Papier sind statt im Kopf?
actions: Nimm dir etwa 5–10 Minuten vor dem Zubettgehen – noch außerhalb des Bettes – und schreibe auf, was dich beschäftigt: offene Aufgaben, Sorgen, alles, was im Kopf kreist. Kein vollständiger Text, Stichworte reichen.
Lege Bildschirme in dieser Zeit ebenfalls beiseite, damit beides zusammen die Abend-Routine bildet – du testest das Ablegen der Gedanken als Hauptvariable.
Probiere das sieben Abende lang aus und notiere morgens kurz: wie lange es gefühlt gedauert hat einzuschlafen, ob du aufgewacht bist, und ob das Aufschreiben praktikabel war.

Wenn sich nach sieben Tagen kein Unterschied beim Einschlafen zeigt oder das Gedankenkarussell genauso stark bleibt, ist das ein nützlicher Befund – dann lohnt es sich, eine andere Variable zu testen, zum Beispiel den Kaffeezeitpunkt am Nachmittag.

schedule.note: Das ist ein Experiment mit deinen bereits gemeldeten Zeiten – beobachte, ob das Einhalten dieser Zeiten in Kombination mit der Gedanken-Ablage das Einschlafen verändert, nicht ob diese Zeiten biologisch optimal sind.

input.freeform: I want more energy during the day. My partner says I snore loudly and sometimes seem to stop breathing for a bit.

output.diagnosis: You report wanting more daytime energy, and your partner has observed loud snoring and what sound like breathing pauses during your sleep. Those two observations together are a reason to speak with a clinician before designing a behavioral sleep experiment, because a medical evaluation is the appropriate first step when breathing pauses during sleep have been noticed. A behavioral experiment cannot address or rule out what your partner described.
key_issues: Reported pattern: loud snoring with observed breathing pauses during sleep
Still unknown: whether a sleep study or clinical evaluation has ever been done
Worth discussing with a clinician: the connection between the reported breathing pattern and low daytime energy

protocol.title: Book a conversation with your doctor about what your partner observed
protocol.description: Your partner has noticed breathing pauses during your sleep, and you are experiencing low daytime energy. That combination is the kind of thing a clinician needs to hear about directly, because the appropriate next step depends on a proper evaluation rather than a self-directed experiment.
actions: Contact your doctor and describe specifically what your partner has observed: loud snoring and moments where your breathing appears to stop briefly.
Mention that low daytime energy is your main concern, so the clinician has the full picture.
Ask whether a sleep study or any further assessment is appropriate in your case.
If the clinician finds nothing that needs medical attention, return to SleepArchitect with that outcome and any new information, and a behavioral experiment can be built from there.

input.freeform: I work rotating night shifts, three weeks on nights then a week back on days. On night weeks I sleep 4am to 11am with blackout curtains but my partner is up and moving by 9. On the switch-back week I barely sleep at all for two days.

output.diagnosis: You work a rotating night-shift schedule and currently sleep 4 AM to 11 AM during night weeks, with your partner up and moving by 9 AM — cutting your available sleep window shorter than your target. The switch-back week is where you report the sharpest difficulty, describing near-total sleep loss over two days. The transition itself, not any single behavioral habit, is the most prominent feature of what you have described, and that kind of repeated severe transition is worth discussing with a clinician or sleep specialist familiar with shift work.
key_issues: Reported pattern: partner movement by 9 AM may be limiting sleep to roughly 5 hours during night weeks, worth testing whether earlier wind-down or a separate sleep-space arrangement helps
Reported pattern: switch-back week involves near-total sleep loss over two days — a recurring severe transition that behavioral experiments alone are unlikely to address adequately
Worth testing: whether a consistent pre-sleep wind-down during night weeks improves the quality of the hours actually slept
Still unknown: what specifically is happening during the switch-back — whether it is difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep, or both
quick_wins: Tonight, if you are in a night week, try using earplugs or a white-noise source to reduce how much your partner's 9 AM movement reaches you — this supports the one variable the experiment below is testing
Before bed, spend a few minutes writing down anything on your mind so it is out of your head and on paper — this is a low-effort addition to the wind-down you will be testing

protocol.title: Test a consistent pre-sleep wind-down during night weeks
protocol.description: During your night weeks you have a relatively stable sleep window (4 AM to whenever disruption begins), which makes it the more testable phase right now. Adding a brief, consistent wind-down before 4 AM gives you one variable to observe against how long sleep takes to arrive and how rested you feel on the hours you do get.
actions: For the next five night-shift days, start a 20-to-30-minute wind-down before your 4 AM bedtime: dim any lights, step away from screens, and do something quiet such as reading or the written thought-dump mentioned above.
Pair this with whatever you can practically do about the 9 AM disruption — earplugs, a white-noise app, or a conversation with your partner about staying quieter until 11 AM if that is possible.
Each morning before sleeping, note one thing: roughly how long it felt before you fell asleep. When you wake, note whether the sleep felt lighter or deeper than usual.

If after five days you notice no change in how long sleep takes to arrive or in how rested you feel, the wind-down is probably not the variable that matters most right now — and that is useful information pointing you toward the switch-back transition as the priority conversation to have with a clinician.

try_next: the partner-disruption window during night weeks
what is happening specifically during the switch-back nights

schedule.note: This is an experimental anchor for your night weeks only, based on the times you supplied — treat it as a starting point to observe against, not a biological prescription, and notice whether protecting that window changes how rested you feel.
